title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Pressure cleaning (all heights)
audience: Owners of small Australian pressure cleaning businesses who need a base rate and a minimum charge before quoting
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from your own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence.
Set a minimum charge for short pressure cleaning jobs, such as a single path or a fence, and explain it before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A pressure cleaning rate depends on the surfaces you clean, how much equipment you carry, whether the work is at height, how far you travel and the range of work you offer. A client who can book a driveway, a path and a house exterior in one visit saves time, which can support a higher rate. A narrow range of basic jobs in a crowded market may need a rate closer to local norms. Use the local evidence in the pressure CP-01 and CP-04 lessons and the BP-05 lesson, not a national average. The lead-generation guide gives a general hourly band of $40 to $100, typical $65 (What's The Damage, verified November 2026). That is an estimate, not a published cost.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Owners often price as though every paid hour can be billed. Travel, quoting, admin, marketing, training, equipment upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate paid hours for a year, then subtract non-billable time to reach billable hours. Jobber puts billable time at about 60 to 80 per cent of working hours (published 5 November 2024, modified 20 July 2026). That is a general range, not an Australian figure, so check your own log against it. If only 60 of every 100 paid hours are billable, the costs of all 100 hours come from the 60, so the rate is about 1.67 times the rate needed for a fully billable week.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, the pressure unit and its upkeep, hoses, detergent, the vehicle, phone, software, marketing and accounting, to the income you need. business.gov.au says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure. Have a registered tax agent confirm how they apply to your situation before the rate is published. Divide the total by billable hours to get the base rate. Review it each quarter, and compare it with what clients accept and with the local evidence.

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short jobs
instruction.body: A single path, a fence panel or a small deck still needs travel, set-up, water connection and runoff control, and those do not shrink with the size of the job. Set a minimum that covers a short visit, and state it before the visit. Contractor+ suggests setting the minimum from the full cost of the visit, divided by one minus the target margin. Its figures are labelled illustrative and are not used here. The lead-generation guide states no minimum charge for pressure cleaning, so the figure must come from your own visit costs. Housecall Pro (country not stated) lists an out-of-area trip fee of $30 to $80; that is not checked for Australia and is not used here.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, admin, marketing, training and leave to find the billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, the pressure unit, hoses, detergent, vehicle, phone, software and marketing.
Add the income you need, with allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by billable hours to find the base rate.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and runoff control for a short job, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative only. A pressure cleaner's log shows that about 60 of every 100 paid hours can be billed, but the owner plans to set the rate as if every paid hour could be billed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the effect on the rate if the wrong assumption is kept?
workedExamples.reasoning: Pricing as if every paid hour were billable understates the rate, because the costs and the income still have to come out of the hours that can be billed. On the owner's own log, the rate is about 1.67 times the rate for a fully billable week. The rate must be built from billable hours, then checked against the lead-generation hourly band and the minimum charge before it is published.

equipmentAndPpe: Log of paid and billable hours for one month
Price sheet with the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a lead-generation band or a competitor's figure without checking your own costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from your own costs and billable hours, then compare it with local evidence.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking short jobs at the same rate, without covering travel, set-up and runoff control.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law. The ACCC says misleading price statements are prohibited, and a single advertised price should show the total including any fee. The ACCC guidance does not cover minimum or call-out charges, or what counts as a fair term. Check those points against current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a price sheet.
Confirm the tax treatment of leave, superannuation and business costs with a registered tax agent.

Runoff control and work at height add time to short jobs. Victoria's runoff and working-at-height rules were not checked in this draft, so check them with EPA Victoria and WorkSafe Victoria before you price those lines.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with local evidence.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short job.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against local evidence.
Set and state a minimum charge for short pressure cleaning jobs.

knowledgeChecks.question: A pressure cleaning owner can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and so the client pays less per job
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average published on a website and from the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay and the owner's own mood on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for a short pressure cleaning job, such as a single path?
options: Because short jobs need travel but no setup time at all and the admin takes no time
Because travel, setup and admin time does not shrink with the size of the job
Because clients expect every job to cost the same amount, whatever its size
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every job the owner takes

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a pressure cleaning base hourly rate?
options: A single published national average from the largest trade body
The owner's own costs and billable hours, compared with local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a bidding site this week

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as super, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure.

Jobber, 'What are billable hours', https://getjobber.com/academy/what-are-billable-hours/, published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026. General range of 60 to 80 per cent billable; not an Australian figure.

AIPT, 'Personal Training Prices: Setting the Right Rates', https://www.aipt.edu.au/articles/personal-training-prices-how-much-should-you-charge, 16 May 2025. Supports: work backwards from a target income; example figures not used.

Contractor+, 'Minimum Service Call Charge: A Contractor's Pricing Guide', https://contractorplus.app/blog/minimum-service-call-charge, 23 September 2026. Supports: minimum set from full visit cost and margin; figures labelled illustrative and not used.
Housecall Pro, 'Flat rate vs hourly', https://www.housecallpro.com/learn/flat-rate-vs-hourly/, published 2 February 2025, updated 7 October 2025. Vendor page; country not stated; trip fee not used.

What's The Damage, 'Pressure washing cost guide', https://whatsthedamage.com.au/pressure-washing-cost/, verified November 2026. Lead-generation hourly band ($40 to $100, typical $65) used as a sense-check only; no minimum charge stated.
ACCC, 'Setting prices: what's allowed', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/pricing/setting-prices-whats-allowed, last modified 15 July 2026. Supports: misleading price statements are prohibited.

Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown. Supports: review prices about every three months.

Work Health and Safety (Managing the Risk of Falls at Workplaces) Code of Practice 2015, https://legislation.gov.au/F2016L00425/asmade/2016-03-30/text/original/epub/OEBPS/document_1/document_1.html, registered 2016. Commonwealth code; not Victorian law. Cited for the height point; the Victorian rule was not checked.

WorkSafe Victoria, news release on falls risks in the solar sector, https://www.worksafe.vic.gov.au/news/2026-08/crackdown-falls-risks-solar-sector, 26 August 2026. Supports: allowing workers onto a roof without adequate protection is unlawful, even with no incident. Aimed at solar; the principle is stated for any roof.
Note: minimum and call-out charge rules, price display beyond the ACCC pricing page, and tax treatment of leave and superannuation are UNCONFIRMED. No pressure-cleaning minimum charge was found.
